answers.change_2023_2026: There have been right protections both in 2023 and 2026 but they are not the same

provisions.instrument: Convención Internacional sobre la Protección de los Derechos de Todos los Trabajadores Migratorios (Ley 26.202)

events.instrument: Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia N° 366/2025
events.what_changed: Art. 6 used to guarantee immigrants and their families equal access to the same protection and rights as nationals, including work and employment, with no qualifier. The new text drops 'y sus familias' and adds 'according to the rights and obligations of each migratory category'. Equal treatment in work now depends on the migrant's category. For migrants authorised to work, equal pay still rests on CN 14 bis and LCT arts. 17/81, which did not change.
events.passage: ARTÍCULO 1°.- Sustitúyese el artículo 6° de la Ley de Migraciones N° 25.871 y sus modificaciones por el siguiente: “ARTÍCULO 6°.- El Estado en todas sus jurisdicciones asegurará el acceso igualitario de los inmigrantes a las mismas condiciones de protección, amparo y derechos de los que gozan los nacionales, de acuerdo con los derechos y obligaciones correspondientes a cada categoría migratoria,

events.instrument: Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia N° 366/2025
events.what_changed: The old art. 53 barred only irregular residents from working. The new text also bars regular residents who are 'not authorised by the migration authority'. This touches who may lawfully work. It does not touch equal pay for those who do work, and art. 56 (labour obligations owed whatever the worker's status) is unchanged.
events.passage: “ARTÍCULO 53.- El extranjero que resida irregularmente en el país, o resida regularmente pero no se encuentre habilitado por la autoridad migratoria, no podrá trabajar o realizar tareas remuneradas o lucrativas, ya sea por cuenta propia o ajena, en relación de dependencia o en forma independiente.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the MRD rated this 'Sometimes; Usually'. The law gives equal pay, but the sources describe heavy informality and labour exploitation of migrants from the region. The 2025 US TIP report, covering 2023–2024, records forced labour of Bolivian, Paraguayan and Peruvian workers in garment work, agriculture and brick-making, and 1,185 labour-trafficking victims identified in 2023. 2026: I found nothing showing that equal-pay enforcement for migrant workers changed. The 2024 TIP data (865 labour-trafficking victims, fewer inspection referrals) and the reports on DNU 366/2025 show more exclusion, but they do not measure wage equality. I kept the rating.

answers.sourcing_note: For Ley 25.871 I read both the InfoLEG original text and the updated text with its amendment notes, and the DNU 366/2025 text in the Boletín Oficial. The 1 January 2023 version is the original art. 6, which Decreto 138/2021 had restored. answers.notes: The answer option stays 'Yes'. I chose 'not the same' because a cited provision (art. 6) was narrowed by the category qualifier, effective 29 May 2025. events.instrument: Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia N° 366/2025
events.what_changed: The new art. 53 bars regular residents 'not authorised' by the migration authority from working. It also makes a migrant irregular if, within the authorised stay, they carry out activities their category does not permit. This ties lawful work more tightly to the category and authorisation granted, which bears on free choice of employment. Art. 23(a) on the temporary migrant worker is unchanged.

answers.implementation_then_now: In both years most labour migrants hold Mercosur-nationality residence (art. 23(l)), which carries open work rights. Only the art. 23(a) temporary worker is tied to the employer named in the application. I found no practice source on how employer changes are actually processed in either period. The documented shift in 2025 is tougher control: new DNM inspection powers (art. 53 bis) and more expulsions (Hivos, 157 in Q1 2025). That shows more enforcement but not denied employer changes. I kept 'Usually' for both dates, with low support.

events.article: Ley 25.871, art. 23 inciso ñ (incorporated by art. 6 DNU)
events.what_changed: Before, the spouse of a temporary resident got temporary residence under the last paragraph of Decreto 616/2010 art. 23; the spouse of a permanent resident got permanent residence under regulation art. 22(b). The DNU creates a statutory 'family reunification' temporary residence for spouses of permanent and temporary residents, for up to 3 years or the principal's term. Art. 51, under which temporary residents may do any paid work during their authorised stay, is unchanged, so the spouse can still work without a separate permit.

events.instrument: Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia N° 366/2025
events.what_changed: Regular residents 'not authorised by the migration authority' may not work. Art. 51 still authorises all temporary residents to work, so a spouse holding a family-reunification residence keeps work rights. The new wording does, however, add an authorisation condition.
events.passage: “ARTÍCULO 53.- El extranjero que resida irregularmente en el país, o resida regularmente pero no se encuentre habilitado por la autoridad migratoria, no podrá trabajar o realizar tareas remuneradas o lucrativas, ya sea por cuenta propia o ajena, en relación de dependencia o en forma independiente.

answers.implementation_then_now: In both periods a spouse admitted as a temporary or permanent resident receives a DNI and residence that carry work rights under art. 51. I found no report of spouses being refused work authorisation. The 2025 reports document harsher residence requirements and family separations through expulsion (Hivos, including an Afro-Uruguayan worker deported after more than 10 years). Those concern access to residence and removal, not the work rights of resident spouses. I kept the rating, with thin evidence.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the MRD rated this 'Sometimes'. The sources document widespread informality and forced-labour conditions among Bolivian, Paraguayan and Peruvian workers in garment work, agriculture, brick-making and domestic work (TIP 2025; 1,185 labour-trafficking victims identified in 2023). 2026: TIP 2025 records 865 labour-trafficking victims in 2024 and fewer labour-inspection trafficking reports (29 against 54 in 2023), plus staffing cuts to the hotline. That suggests weaker enforcement capacity, but not clearly a different level for migrant workers, so I kept 'Sometimes'. The general labour reform (Ley 27.802) came in March 2026, after the window.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The citation should name LCT art. 17, which bans discrimination between workers on grounds of nationality; it is the most direct labour-law basis. Decreto 616/2010 arts. 5, 6 and 56 are not substantive provisions on this point.

answers.change_2023_2026: There have been right protections both in 2023 and 2026 but the implementation level of these protections has changed

events.what_changed: The government dissolved the national anti-discrimination, xenophobia and racism institute (INADI), which handled complaints and promotion work against discrimination, including against migrants. The ban itself (Ley 25.871 art. 13) is unchanged; this affects enforcement, not the protection answer.
events.passage: ARTÍCULO 1°.- Disuélvese el INSTITUTO NACIONAL CONTRA LA DISCRIMINACIÓN, LA XENOFOBIA Y EL RACISMO (INADI), organismo descentralizado actuante en el ámbito del MINISTERIO DE JUSTICIA.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: at Argentina's April 2023 review, CERD members raised persistent structural discrimination against migrants and continued racial profiling of migrants by police. INADI was then active and led the delegation, so 'Sometimes' fits. 2026: INADI was dissolved by Decreto 696/2024, leaving complaints to the courts. Civil-society reporting on DNU 366/2025 (Hivos/EU SEE, August 2025) documents official rhetoric linking migration to crime and a record pace of expulsions in early 2025 (157 in Q1). It also notes a disproportionate impact on trans people, sex workers and Afro-descendant migrants. I lower the rating to 'Rarely; Sometimes' on the strength of this institutional and practice shift.
